newsitem.title: USA: N.Y.S. Senate wants $2.5 bln of business tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: N.Y.S. Senate wants $2.5 bln of business tax cuts.

text.p: The New York State Senate, pointing to a recent string of budget surpluses, said on Wednesday it had approved its own plan to cut business taxes by $2.5 billion over five years.

Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno said that big tax reductions had turned the state's economy around, noting that, in fiscal 1997, which ended on March 31, it posted a surplus of over $1.8 billion, while over the past three years, 164,000 new jobs had been created and "hundreds of thousands" of other positions saved.
"Three consecutive years of tax cuts have helped increase revenues to the state," said Bruno in prepared remarks.
"The truth is, New York cannot afford not to cut taxes."

The Senate's business tax cut plan, called "Jobs for the 21st Century Business Tax Cut, would cut such taxes by $216 million this year. Coupled with a five-year, $3 billion plan to reduce school taxes, the new plan would slash how much taxpayers are on the hook for by more than $5.5 billion.

However, the Senate's huge tax cuts were blasted by the minority Democrats in the Senate, who pointed out the Republicans had criticized their plan to spend nearly the same amount over the same period on school aid.

In a reversal, the Assembly, which is controlled by Democrats, approved its own version of a budget, a step the Senate took last year, but did not repeat this year. For the 13th year in a row, the state started a new fiscal year without a budget in place.

"The major difference is that the Assembly Democrats have had the courage to pass an entire budget," said Martin Connor, the Senate Minority Leader. "Republican Senators admitted today that they won't approve the Pataki budget, but there still is no restoration for education or healthcare."
The Assembly rejected all but $96 million of roughly $820 million of healthcare cuts proposed by the Republican governor and also has criticized his plan to raise tuition at state universities.

Connor forecast that school districts again would have to take out costly, short-term loans because the state was unlikley to get a new budget before a six-week contingency budget ends. The state's perenially late budgets also raises its borrowing costs.

One of the Senate's proposed tax cuts that could prove the most popular, if Gov George Pataki and the Democrat-led Assembly agreed to it, was a plan to cut the state sales tax on clothing, a step that eventually would cost New York State $550 million. A one-week moratorium in January, which was matched by most localities, boosted sales, according to local officials, including New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani.

The Senate's plan would exempt items of clothing that cost less than $500 during one back-to-school week in August and again in January 1998. The state's four percent levy then would be phased out at the rate of one percent a year, a schedule localities could match if they chose.
The Gross Receipts Tax on utilities would be phased out and utility taxes frozen for 1997, at an ultimate cost of $710 million. New York State has among the highest energy rates in the country.

Healthcare providers also would get the benefit of a phased-out Gross Receipts Tax, which was estimated to cost the state $550 million. Gift and estate taxes would be lowered, in an effort to give more senior citizens and retirees an incentive to remain residents, at a cost of $300 million.
